title: Review 4: Piqué, stripes, colour effects and cover

quizzes.title: Key terms across the lectures
quizzes.intro: Terms from the cord, pattern and cover lectures.

questions.q: A piqué (welt) is made with
options: One warp and two wefts only
A face warp and a tightly held stitching warp
questions.explain: The tight stitching ends pull the face down in lines, and the face bulges between them.

questions.q: Wadding picks in a piqué are
options: Thick picks laid between face and back to fill the cords
Picks that weave plain with the face
questions.explain: They do not show; they pad the cord so it stands up more.

questions.q: A stripe design changes weave
questions.explain: Different weaves sit side by side across the warp. A check changes across the picks as well.

questions.q: A colour-and-weave effect is a pattern produced by
options: The order of coloured yarns together with a simple weave
questions.explain: The face shows warp colour where the end is up and weft colour where the pick is on top.

questions.q: Hound’s tooth is made with
options: A 2/2 twill with four dark and four light threads in warp and weft
questions.explain: The 4-and-4 colouring on a 2/2 twill gives the broken-check, dog-tooth shape.

questions.q: Relative cover of a set of threads is
questions.explain: Diameter over spacing: the fraction of the spacing filled by yarn.

questions.q: A cover factor K of 2,670 (K = threads per 100 mm × √tex) means the threads of that set are touching.
questions.explain: At that value d ÷ p = 1.

questions.q: “Clean cut” at the join of two weaves means
options: Warp floats of one weave meet weft floats of the other, giving a sharp line
questions.explain: Opposing floats at the boundary stop threads sliding across and blurring the edge.

questions.q: In a piqué the stitching ends are usually in the proportion of
options: One stitching end to two face ends
Two stitching ends to one face end
questions.explain: Welt piqué is threaded face, stitching, face: one stitching end for every two face ends.

questions.q: The cords of a plain welt piqué run across the cloth.
questions.explain: The stitching ends lift on certain picks, making furrows weft-way; Bedford cords run the other way.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: Why stripes pucker, lines turn and cover adds up the way it does.

questions.q: Two weaves placed side by side in a stripe should interlace with similar frequency because otherwise
options: One stripe takes up more warp and the cloth puckers
questions.explain: Different interlacing gives different crimp and tension; the tighter stripe pulls the cloth out of flat.

questions.q: In plain weave with warp dark-light and weft light-dark, fine lines run warp-way. Shifting the weft colour order by one pick
questions.explain: The same weave now brings dark over dark in rows instead of columns.

questions.q: Cloth cover is C₁ + C₂ − C₁C₂ and not simply C₁ + C₂ because
options: Where warp and weft cross, the same area would be counted twice
questions.explain: The product is the area covered by both sets at once.

questions.q: Raising the tension of the stitching warp in a piqué makes the cords
questions.explain: A tighter stitching end pulls the face deeper into the furrow.

questions.q: If the stitching points of a piqué are moved diagonally from one repeat to the next, the furrows
questions.explain: This is the waved piqué of the lecture.

questions.q: Doubling the tex of a yarn at the same threads per 100 mm multiplies its cover factor by
questions.explain: K = n √tex, and √2 ≈ 1.41.

questions.q: A check differs from a stripe in that
options: The weave (or colour) changes in both the warp and the weft direction
questions.explain: Blocks are formed by changing across the ends and across the picks.

questions.q: The same 2/2 twill weave can give quite different patterns when only the colour order of the yarns is changed.
questions.explain: That is the whole idea of colour-and-weave effects: the lifting plan stays, the colours move.

questions.q: A cloth has warp cover 1.0. Whatever the weft cover, the cloth cover is
questions.explain: 1 + C₂ − 1 × C₂ = 1: the warp alone already hides everything.

questions.q: In a colour-and-weave effect, where a dark end is lifted over a light pick you see light on the face.
questions.explain: The lifted end is on top, so you see its colour: dark.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Cover, spacing and repeat sizes to calculate.

questions.q: A warp of 25 tex has 280 ends per 100 mm. What is its cover factor K = n √tex?
A set of threads has K = 1,335. What is its relative cover, to two decimals? (maximum K = 2,670)
Warp cover is 0.50 and weft cover 0.75. What is the cloth cover, to three decimals?
There are 250 threads per 100 mm. What is the thread spacing in mm, to one decimal?
A yarn of 36 tex is set at a spacing of 0.30 mm. What is its relative cover, to two decimals? Use d = √tex ÷ 26.7.
A welt piqué is threaded face, stitching, face, and so on. In a warp of 3,600 ends, how many are stitching ends?
questions.explain: One end in every three: 3,600 ÷ 3 = 1,200.

questions.q: A colour order of 4 dark, 4 light is used with a 2/2 twill (4-end repeat). How many ends are in the pattern repeat?
questions.explain: The colour repeat is 8 and the weave repeat 4, so the pattern repeats on 8 ends.

questions.q: A colour order of 3 dark, 3 light is used with a 2/2 twill (4-end repeat). How many ends are in the pattern repeat?
questions.explain: The least common multiple of 6 and 4 is 12.

questions.q: A check has blocks of 24 and 12 ends, and 24 and 12 picks. How many squares of point paper does one repeat cover?
How many threads of 25 tex per 100 mm would give full cover (K = 2,670)?
questions.explain: 2,670 ÷ 5 = 534 threads per 100 mm.

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: A coloured shirting: how well it covers, and what pattern its colours make.

questions.q: What is the warp cover factor?
What is the weft cover factor?
What is the relative cover of the warp, to two decimals?
What is the relative cover of the weft, to two decimals?
What is the cloth cover, to two decimals?
What is the diameter of the warp yarn in mm, to two decimals?
What is the spacing of the warp threads in mm, to two decimals?
With this colouring on plain weave, the face of the cloth shows
options: Fine hairlines of dark and light
questions.explain: One-and-one colouring on plain weave lines the same colour up in fine stripes.

questions.q: The designer wants the hairlines to run the other way. The simplest change is to
options: Shift the weft colour order by one pick
questions.explain: Starting the weft with dark instead of light turns the lines without touching the weave or the warp.

questions.q: About 18% of the area of this cloth is open space between the threads.
questions.explain: Cloth cover is about 0.82, so roughly 0.18 of the area is not covered by yarn.

quizzes.case: A plain-weave shirting has a warp of 16 tex at 400 ends per 100 mm and a weft of 25 tex at 300 picks per 100 mm. The warp is coloured one end dark, one end light; the weft is one pick light, one pick dark. Use d = √tex ÷ 26.7 mm and a maximum cover factor of 2,670.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Mixed questions on structure, pattern and cover.

questions.q: Which pair of weaves is the safest to combine in a stripe without puckering?
questions.explain: The two twills interlace equally often and have the same pick repeat; only the direction differs.

questions.q: A cloth must have a cloth cover of at least 0.90. The warp cover is 0.75. What is the smallest weft cover that achieves it, to two decimals?
A 16 tex warp has a cover factor of 1,600. If the yarn is changed to 25 tex at the same threads per 100 mm, what is the new cover factor?
In a plain welt piqué, on a face pick the stitching ends are
questions.explain: They stay under the face cloth and rise over it only on the stitching (indent) picks.

questions.q: A hound’s tooth uses 4 dark and 4 light threads in both warp and weft at 80 ends per inch. How many pattern repeats are there in one inch of width?
questions.explain: The pattern repeat is 8 ends: 80 ÷ 8 = 10 repeats per inch.

questions.q: A stripe of plain weave beside a stripe of 3/1 twill is to be woven from one beam. A likely problem is
options: The plain stripe takes up more warp, so its ends become tight
The twill stripe cannot be dented
questions.explain: Plain weave interlaces at every pick and uses more warp length than the twill, so tension differs across the stripes.

questions.q: Two cloths with the same cloth cover must have the same weight.
questions.explain: Cover depends on diameter and spacing. A cloth of fine yarns closely set can cover as well as a heavier one of coarse yarns.

questions.q: A check appears in a single colour of yarn when
options: Blocks of different weaves reflect light differently
questions.explain: Plain blocks look flat and twill or rib blocks lustrous, so the weave change alone shows as a check.

questions.q: A piqué has 96 face ends per inch and one stitching end for every two face ends. How many ends per inch are there in total?
questions.explain: 96 face + 48 stitching = 144 ends per inch.

questions.q: On a 2/2 twill with a colour order of 2 dark, 2 light in both directions, the pattern repeat is
questions.explain: Colour repeat 4 and weave repeat 4 coincide, so the pattern repeats on 4 ends.
